newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile tries again to curb armed forces' clout.
newsitem.headline: Chile tries again to curb armed forces' clout.

text.p: Chile, in a bid by democratic leaders to curb the armed forces' influence in politics, sent a law to Congress on Tuesday to change its constitution by abolishing nine military-appointed senators.
Three ministers presented deputies with the bill seeking to sweep away some of the most controversial legacies of Gen. Augusto Pinochet's regime that ruled Chile for 17 years.
"It is not fair that 20 percent of the Senate is made up of people who are appointed and do not represent the population," Interior Minister Carlos Figueroa told lawmakers in the port of Valparaiso.
"The country has advanced in terms of its institutions and economy, but this anti-democratic institution lingers on as a remnant," he said.

The designated senators hold the balance of power in the Senate and have often allied themselves with rightist opposition parties to block laws proposed by the government, including earlier bids to reform the constitution.

Under the 1980 military-dictated constitution, nine of the country's 47 senators are not elected. Two are named by the president, three by the supreme court with four appointed indirectly by the armed forces.
Those senators have been an ongoing source of embarrassment for President Eduardo Frei's government, which is keen to promote Chile as being fully democratic.
Despite the failure of two previous attempts to change the constitution since Chile returned to democratic rule in 1990, the government is confident that this time it will succeed, Figueroa said.

The government hopes the rightist Renovacion Nacional party will support the plan as they realise that the right's influence over the appointments will be considerably weaker in future, socialist deputy Jaime Estevez said.
"But if we don't succeed now, we will try for a fourth, fifth and sixth time as it is a matter of principle that all members of parliament are elected," Estevez said.
The pro-military Union Democrata Independiente party has said it will vote against the changes.
